narrative:
The model estimates a 52% chance that you will leave your job, which is just over the threshold for predicting departure. Because of this, the company has decided not to offer you the promotion at this time.

Three factors stood out most in the model’s reasoning. First, your total years of professional experience had the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward you staying. At 1–5 years, you are in the most common group among employees the model expects to remain, so the system sees this as a stabilizing factor. 

The second most important factor worked in the opposite direction. Having received other job offers while at the company strongly pulled the prediction toward leaving. This signal suggested you may have attractive external opportunities that increase the likelihood you will move on.

Your length of time with this specific organization ranked third and also nudged the prediction toward leaving. Like your overall experience, you fall into the 1–5 year bracket, which is the largest group among those expected to stay; however, the model interpreted your relatively short tenure here as indicating you are still in an early, more mobile phase of your time with the firm.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and shorter organizational tenure slightly outweighed the stabilizing effect of your broader experience, tipping the prediction just above 50%. 

The organization should consider discussing your career goals and any external offers with you directly. You may want to reflect on whether your current role aligns with your longer-term plans and whether additional support, such as training or clearer promotion paths, could change your outlook.
